summary: This note is a collection of passages from a Wikipedia-style article on dialects and the distinction between dialects and languages. It covers Ukraine's history under the German Empire and the USSR and the Ukrainization process, North African Darija versus Literary Arabic, Sardinian and other Italo-Dalmatian varieties, the Tuscan roots of standard Italian, Kloss's abstand and ausbau framework, and the Ukrainian-Russian boundary with Surzhyk. It also discusses why no universal criterion separates languages from dialects, using Limón Creole, English and Serbo-Croatian as examples, and closes with dialect use in German-speaking Switzerland.
one_line: Wikipedia-derived note on the dialect-versus-language distinction, with examples from Arabic, Italian, Ukrainian, English, Serbo-Croatian and Swiss German.
key_facts: Heinz Kloss developed the abstand and ausbau framework in 1967 to describe speech communities.
The Tsarist Government of the Russian Empire claimed in the 19th century that Ukrainian was merely a dialect of Russian.
An intermediate dialect between Ukrainian and Russian, called Surzhyk, has developed in Ukraine.
Darijas are sometimes considered more different from other Arabic dialects in Tunisia, Algeria, and Morocco.
North African countries officially prefer Literary Arabic, the liturgical language of Islam and the language of the Qur'an.
Since the 1960s, Darijas have been occupying an increasing use in theatre, film, music, television, advertisement, social media, folk-tale books and company names.
The Sardinian language is considered its own Romance language family, separate from standard Italian and the wider Italo-Dalmatian family.
Gallurese, Sassarese, and Corsican are spoken in Sardinia and are considered Italo-Dalmatian languages.
The Tuscan-based language that became modern standard Italian had been used in poetry and literature since at least the 12th century.
Dante Alighieri, Giovanni Boccaccio, Niccolò Machiavelli, and Petrarch helped make Tuscan-based Italian widely known in Italy.
Limón Creole is spoken on the Caribbean coast of Costa Rica by descendants of Jamaican people.
British and American English are almost universally regarded as dialects of a single language, while Serbian and Croatian are treated by some regional linguists as distinct languages.
Swiss German dialects are the default everyday language in virtually every situation in Switzerland and Liechtenstein, whereas standard German is seldom spoken.
Some Swiss German speakers perceive standard German to be a foreign language.
Dialect use is less common in Northern Germany than in the South, in cities than in the countryside, and in public than in familiar environments.
